title: A Study of 39,000 Women Found That Two Hours of Brisk Walking Per Week Cuts Stroke Risk by 30 Per Cent. Running Did Not Do Better.
excerpt: The Women's Health Study tracked participants for twelve years. Brisk walking outperformed vigorous exercise for stroke prevention. South Asian women in the US have among the lowest physical activity rates of any demographic group.
body:
A twelve-year study of nearly 39,000 women has found that brisk walking for at least two hours per week reduces stroke risk by approximately 30 per cent — and that vigorous activities like running and swimming did not produce meaningfully better results for stroke prevention specifically.

The findings, drawn from the Women's Health Study and reported by the American Heart Association, are significant for a simple reason: walking is the most accessible form of exercise on earth. It requires no equipment, no gym membership, no particular fitness level, and no cultural barrier. For South Asian women in the US — a population with some of the lowest physical activity rates in the country — the data carries particular weight.

## What the Study Found

Researchers analysed physical activity data from 39,000 female health professionals aged 45 and older, following them for twelve years. Women who walked briskly for at least two hours per week had a roughly 30 per cent lower risk of stroke compared to women who did not walk regularly. The brisk pace was the key variable — leisurely strolling did not produce the same protective effect.

What surprised the researchers was that more intense exercise did not significantly outperform brisk walking for stroke outcomes. Running, swimming, and cycling are beneficial for cardiovascular health in other ways, but for the specific endpoint of stroke prevention, the walking cohort did nearly as well. The American Heart Association recommends 2.5 hours of moderate-intensity exercise per week; this study suggests that walking alone can meet that threshold and deliver measurable protection.

## Why This Matters for South Asian Women

South Asian women in the United States face a compounding set of health risks that make this finding especially relevant. A community-based study of physical activity among South Asian Indian immigrant women found that cultural norms, family obligations, safety concerns, and lack of culturally appropriate exercise options all contribute to lower activity levels. Many women who emigrated from India grew up in households where structured exercise was not part of the daily routine.

The cardiovascular risk profile for South Asians in America is already elevated. A Northwestern University study found that South Asian adults face elevated heart risks at age 45 despite reporting healthier dietary habits than other groups, with higher rates of prediabetes, diabetes, and hypertension. For women specifically, stroke risk compounds these vulnerabilities — and the protective factor identified in this study is one that does not require a treadmill, a personal trainer, or even a dedicated hour at the gym.

Two hours of brisk walking per week translates to roughly 17 minutes per day. That is a walk to the neighbourhood grocery store and back. A loop around the apartment complex after dinner. A morning circuit of the park before the children wake up.

## The Acculturation Factor

Research from the MASALA study — the largest longitudinal study of South Asian cardiovascular health in the US — has shown that acculturation patterns directly influence health behaviours. Higher levels of social integration and community connection correlate with better health outcomes. But acculturation also brings dietary shifts: more processed food, more sedentary work, more screen time.

Walking is one intervention that cuts across acculturation levels. It does not require English proficiency, familiarity with gym culture, or disposable income. In India, walking is the default mode of transportation for millions. The irony is that emigration to the US — where car dependence is the norm — eliminates the incidental walking that many women did without thinking about it as exercise.

For Indian-American families, the study offers a practical conversation starter. The data is not ambiguous: brisk walking for two hours a week provides stroke protection comparable to more demanding forms of exercise. For mothers, grandmothers, and aunties who may resist the idea of joining a gym or taking up running, walking is familiar, dignified, and now backed by one of the largest women's health studies ever conducted.

## The Practical Prescription

The American Heart Association recommends 150 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise per week. This study shows that brisk walking alone can fulfil that prescription and deliver a 30 per cent reduction in stroke risk. The key word is brisk — a pace that raises your heart rate, makes conversation slightly effortful, and covers about a mile in 15 to 20 minutes.

For South Asian women navigating the gap between traditional lifestyles and American sedentary culture, the prescription is clear: walk fast, walk often, and do not wait for a gym membership to start.
